questions.stem: Choose the correct word: 'The court will ___ on the bail application next week.' (accept/except/expect)
questions.explanation: D is correct. The sentence means the court will deliver a decision/ruling. ACCEPT = to receive; EXCEPT = excluding; EXPECT = to anticipate. None of these fits 'rule on the bail application'. The correct verb is 'RULE' (the court will rule on the application = deliver a decision). This tests attention to context — exam questions sometimes include plausible distractors that are wrong words for the context, and 'None of these' or 'No improvement' can be the correct answer. Trap: 'expect' sounds vaguely appropriate but means the court anticipates something, not delivers a ruling.

questions.stem: Choose the correct word: 'The committee passed a ___ banning the use of single-use plastics.' (statue / statute / stature)
questions.explanation: B is correct. STATUTE = a written law passed by a legislative body. 'The committee passed a STATUTE' = the committee enacted a law. STATUE = a carved or cast figure (monument). STATURE = a person's height or high regard ('a man of great stature'). STATIONARY = not moving (as opposed to stationery = writing materials). Trap: Statue vs Statute is a common SSC confusable pair — statue is the monument, statute is the law.

questions.stem: Choose the correct word: 'She wrote the letter on official ___.' (stationary / stationery)
questions.explanation: B is correct. STATIONERY (noun, ends in -ERY) = writing materials (paper, envelopes, pens). 'Official stationery' = official letterhead paper. STATIONARY (adjective, ends in -ARY) = not moving; still. Memory trick: stationERY has E, like papEr and pEn (writing materials); stationARY has A, like stAy (staying still). Trap: confusing the -ary/-ery endings is a classic SSC vocabulary error; remember stationery=paper/pen, stationary=still.

questions.stem: Choose the correct word: 'The accused was charged with ___ for deliberately destroying evidence.' (contempt / contemptuous / contention)
questions.explanation: A is correct. CONTEMPT (noun) = the offence of being disobedient to or disrespectful of a court. 'Charged with contempt (of court)' = charged for showing disrespect to the court (destroying evidence). CONTEMPTUOUS (adjective) = showing contempt; disrespectful. CONTENTION = a point made in an argument; a competitive situation. CONTEMPTUOUSNESS = the quality of being contemptuous (a noun, but the legal charge is 'contempt'). The legal phrase is 'contempt of court', not 'contemptuousness of court'.

questions.stem: Choose the correct word: 'The scientists ___ the ancient fossils to determine their age.' (dated / data / datum / dated)
questions.explanation: A is correct. DATED (verb) = determined the age of; assigned a date to. 'Scientists DATED the fossils' = they determined how old the fossils were (carbon dating etc.). DATA = facts/information (plural of datum); DATUM = a single data point; DOTED = to be excessively fond of someone. Only 'dated' works as a past-tense verb meaning 'determined the age of'. Trap: 'data' sounds close to 'dated' and seems related to scientific process, but 'the scientists data the fossils' is grammatically wrong.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses PRINCIPAL and PRINCIPLE correctly?

options.option_text: The principle of the school gave a speech; honesty is our principal value.
The principal of the school gave a speech; honesty is our principle value.
The principal of the school gave a speech; honesty is our principal value.
The principal of the school gave a speech; honesty is our core principle.

questions.explanation: D is correct. PRINCIPAL = noun (the head of a school; the main party in a transaction) OR adjective (main/chief). PRINCIPLE = noun only (a rule, belief, or standard). Correct usage: 'principal of the school' (noun = head) + 'core principle' (noun = rule/standard). Option A uses 'principle' (rule) for the school head — wrong. Option B uses 'principle value' where 'principle' is wrongly used as an adjective (only 'principal' can be an adjective). Option C uses 'principal value' correctly but misses the distinction. D uses 'principal' (head) + 'principle' (rule) correctly in separate phrases. Memory trick: 'princip_A_l' = school head, like the _A_dministrator.

questions.stem: Choose the correct homophone pair: 'The ___ (1) sent a strong ___ (2) to the rebel group.' Use: MASSAGE / MESSAGE / MASSAGE
questions.explanation: B is correct. MESSAGE = a written or verbal communication. MASSAGE = a physical manipulation of muscles. 'Sent a strong MESSAGE to the rebel group' = communicated a warning or signal. 'Sent a massage' = sent a muscle-rubbing service (nonsensical in context). This is a basic homophone pair that SSC frequently tests. Message and massage are not exact homophones but are commonly confused in written form.

questions.stem: Choose the correct word: 'The historical document was written in ___ to prevent public disclosure.' (cypher / cipher / siphon)
questions.explanation: A is correct. CIPHER (also spelled CYPHER, British variant) = a secret code used to disguise information. 'Written in cipher' = encoded to prevent unauthorised reading. SIPHON = a tube used to draw liquid from a container by suction. The two words sound completely different (SY-fur vs SY-fon) but are often confused in spelling-heavy questions. 'Cipher code' is redundant (cipher = code). The correct answer is A (cypher/cipher = the encoded writing).

questions.stem: Choose the correct word: 'A good negotiator must know when to ___ a point and when to stand firm.' (seed / cede / seize / siege)
questions.explanation: B is correct. CEDE = to give up, surrender, or yield (territory, a point in negotiation, or a right). 'Know when to cede a point' = know when to concede/yield on a point. SEED = a plant embryo. SEIZE = to take hold of quickly and firmly. SIEGE = a military operation surrounding a place to force its surrender. All four words have the 'see' sound but different spellings and meanings. Cede is specifically used for yielding/surrendering in formal/diplomatic contexts.

questions.stem: Choose the correct word: 'The old building has been ___ since the earthquake.' (vacant / vacated / vacation / vacate)
questions.explanation: A is correct. VACANT (adjective) = empty; not occupied. 'The building HAS BEEN vacant' = the building IS (currently) empty, has been in that state since the earthquake. VACATED (past participle of vacate = to leave) would give 'has been vacated' = has been emptied/left, but this means someone actively left it, not just that it's empty. VACATION = a holiday. VACATE = to leave or give up (verb in base form). The adjective 'vacant' is needed here to describe the building's current state. 'Has been vacant' = present perfect state: continuously empty since the earthquake.
